paragraphs.heading: What coastal geography covers
paragraphs.text: Coastal geography studies the region where ocean meets land, a region that never stops changing. It takes in the physical geography of the coast and its human geography as well. Part of the work is understanding how the coast is weathered, particularly by wave action, by moving sediment and by the weather. Another part is understanding how people interact with the coast.

paragraphs.heading: Strong waves and weak waves
paragraphs.text: Waves strike the shoreline constantly, and they are the main force that moves and shapes the coastline. What a wave does depends on its strength. Strong waves, also known as destructive waves, belong to winter and to high-energy beaches. They leave less sediment on the beach, because they carry it out to bars under the sea. Weak waves, called constructive waves, come mostly in summer and belong to low-energy beaches. They do the reverse: they heap sediment onto the berm, and the beach grows.

paragraphs.heading: How sand travels along a beach
paragraphs.text: Longshore drift is the steady movement of sediment along a beach by wave action. It happens because waves meet the shore at an angle. A wave lifts sediment, such as sand, and carries it along the beach on a slant; this is called swash. Gravity then pulls the water back at a right angle to the beach, and the water drops its load as it loses energy; this is called backwash. The following wave lifts the sediment again and pushes it a little further along. The outcome is a continual flow of sediment in one direction.

paragraphs.heading: What longshore drift builds
paragraphs.text: River mouths are the main sources of beach sediment. Longshore drift is the reason that long strips of coast are covered in sediment, and not only the areas near those river mouths. The process relies on rivers supplying sediment constantly. If the supply stops, beaches further along the shore can be left bare. Longshore drift helps create many landforms, among them barrier islands, bay beaches and spits. In general it tends to straighten the coast: barriers cut bays off from the sea, sediment usually collects in bays, and sediment is carried away from exposed headlands.

paragraphs.heading: Wind, rain and salt
paragraphs.text: Weather shapes the coast too. Winds blowing onshore lift sand and move it up the beach, where it forms dunes. Rain erodes rocks on the shore and carries the weathered material down to the shoreline, where it forms beaches. On beaches, the main physical weathering process is the growth of salt crystals. Salt spray is carried by the wind onto rocks and soaks into their small pores and cracks. The water then evaporates and the salt crystallises, which creates pressure and often breaks the rock down.

paragraphs.heading: When the sea itself rises
paragraphs.text: Sea level on Earth regularly goes up and down as the climate changes. In cold periods, more of the planet's water is locked up as ice in glaciers. In warm periods that water is released, and the sea rises and covers more land. Rising sea levels form fjords and rias. A fjord is a glacial valley that has been flooded, and a ria is a river valley that has been flooded. Fjords typically have steep, rocky sides.
